II further chooses the majority pronunciation within the city (keeping n-/l- and initial ng-, not following the Saikwaan style) (a named variety of the language); data: Preface…
5107.tone: Chao treats Cantonese as a tone language: the page preceding section 13 discusses the changed tone pinn'iam ('a large number of parallel cases of pinn'iam in Cantonese', p. 36), and section 5 'Tones' (p. 23) and section 7 'Tone Sandhi' (p. 26) treat the tones and section 12 'Changed Tone or Pinn'iam' (pp. 34-36) the changed tones. Section 13 then denies word stress outright and contrasts Cantonese with Mandarin and English, where stress is word-constituting. Prominence is sentence-level and stylistic (focus), consistent with Man 2002 and Bauer et al. 2004 (focus-stress cued mainly by duration) and with Wong, Chan & Beckman 2005 abstract ('absence of contrast between stressed and reduced (neutral tone) syllables').

In the traditional order of reckoning, the three types are called the Even Tone, the Rising Tone, and the Going Tone ... 5109.heavy: Closed syllables: 'penultimate closed syllables' (ta-báshti, ta-búyta, ta-búybu) and 'an initial heavy syllable' (púydara, bállata, the latter with a base-generated geminate /l:/); gemination of the following consonant is used 'to make the stress-avoiding syllable heavy' (dójjo 'body', tí-bba 'my husband'); Spanish loans optionally insert a coda (basu ~ bajsu) in the stressed syllable. No vowel-length criterion is stated for weight.
5109.dflt: Left-to-right iambic footing with final-syllable extrametricality: primary on the rightmost foot head = penult in odd-syllable words, antepenult in even-syllable words of four or more, first syllable in disyllables (primary-only grids 2..8: 10 010 0100 00010 000100 0000010 00000100), earlier foot heads secondary; overridden by stress-attracting prefixes (tá-sibë 'our house' vs ti-síbë 'my house') and by diacritically marked roots.
5109.prule: Default: iambic (right-headed) binary feet built from the left edge of the word with the final syllable extrametrical; primary stress on the head of the rightmost foot, so penult in odd-syllable words (pojóre 'canoe', three syllables) and antepenult in even-syllable words of four or more (tipójore 'my canoe', four syllables), a disyllable being stressed on its first syllable (mála); primary stress never leaves a two-syllable right-edge window (ti-memé-shama, tàlipá-newe). Weight override: a closed (heavy) penult takes stress over foot structure and over stress-attracting prefixes (ta-báshti 'our wife'); a heavy initial syllable in an unaffixed trisyllable takes stress (púydara, bállata); a heavy antepenult is otherwise ignored to avoid clash (aròpajtíya); heavy penult beats heavy antepenult (i-shojtó-jti-ø-w). Author hedges: 'Further research is needed to determine the exact role heaviness plays'.
5109.srule: All foot heads are stressed and only the rightmost is primary, so every earlier foot head carries secondary stress: with iambs counted from the left edge and the final syllable extrametrical (unstressable for secondary as for primary stress), secondary stress falls by default on the 2nd (and 4th) syllable from the left (a-jàmisá-jti-ø=ya, achàmatíjsha; 2014 yurùjaré-tu, ti-pòjoré-ni); lexically footed stress-attracting prefixes (ta-, pa-, ma-, ka-, li-, la-, co-operative object prefixes) and closed syllables form feet of their own and keep secondary stress when a later head is primary (tà-pojóre, tà-sibë́=chi, tà-pantálu, 2014 òtto-máshi-tu); adjacent heavy/stress-attracting syllables are not both stressed (clash avoidance). Same footing in compounds (tàlipá-newe).

5110.dq: En yurutí las raíces verbales se componen de una a tres sílabas y no poseen un acento fijo, sino que éste varía bajo influencia de los morfemas que se le sufijan. (p.48) — cf. p.37: 'cuando hay una relajación en el patrón de acentuación en la palabra donde se encuentra'; Barnes 1999 p.212: 'one accented syllable per phonological word'.
5110.dloc: sec. 7.1 'Fonética y Fonología', p.31; sec. 7.3 'Resumen', pp.39-40; sec. 8.1.2 'El Verbo', p.48.
5110.prule: No positional stress rule is stated. The only first-hand open source reports isolated lexical pitch contrasts (author unsure whether tonal or accentual: guacamaya [mã:˥] 'macaw' vs camino [mã:˧] 'path'), says accentual patterns were identified but not characterised, and states that verb roots have no fixed accent: the accent moves under the influence of the suffixes attached. Family surveys code Yurutí as a two-level pitch/tone system (Ardila 1998: two phonological pitch levels, YR dii 'sangre' vs díí 'carne'; Barnes 1999, from Kinch & Kinch ms: pitch accent, one accented (high-pitched) syllable per phonological word). Coded as a tone/pitch-accent system with no stress rule.
5110.srule: None stated. Barnes 1999 (family survey, Yurutí data second-hand from Kinch & Kinch ms): 'Some of the languages, such as Desano, Tuyuca, Yuruti and Cubeo, have one accented syllable per phonological word' (no secondary or alternating accent, unlike Secoya). Not mentioned in Valencia Pérez 2014 (ch. 7 'Fonología' pp.31-40 and sec. 8.1.2 p.48 read).

No he realizado aún un estudio de este fenómeno fonológico en la lengua yurutí por no encontrar más de dos ejemplos que lo ilustren y porque no predice cambios al análisis de la estrategia MOD. 5111.prule: No reachable source states a stress rule for Yutanduchi de Guerrero Mixtec. The only statement whose scope formally covers the variety is Josserand's (1983:180) definition of the Mixtec couplet as 'composed of two syllables and carrying stress on the first of these two', seen second-hand only: Carroll 2015:86 reads it as generalizing across the modern varieties of Josserand's survey (Yutanduchi = survey town Yutn, Table A.2 p. 276), Penner 2019:92 reads it as posited for Proto-Mixtec, and Carroll 2015:87 names Yoloxochitl as a Mixtec variety with final stress, so the generalization is not exceptionless. Carroll's variety-by-variety survey (p. 86: Nuxaa, Ayutla, Jicaltepec, Acatlan, Diuxi, Mixtepec, Atatlahuca, Silacayoapan, Alacatlatzala) does not include Yutanduchi, and McKendry 2001, the only reachable work with first-hand Yutanduchi data, says nothing about its stress. If the catalog ever admits the family-level statement as a proxy for the variety, the position is couplet-initial (first syllable of the disyllabic root; root-anchored, quantity-insensitive), which is set by morphology rather than fixed and quantity-insensitive, since it is defined on the couplet and not counted from a word edge.

Wannemacher 1998 (Google Books, grade excerpt, not the record's basis): 'Zaiwa word-level stress is appropriate since stress is relevant in determining syllable structure. Stress is manifest as acoustic intensity, full vowel quality, and vowel length and does not necessarily correspond to pitch'; 'Zaiwa stressed syllables are the unmarked case. Unstressed syllables are the marked case, occurring with peripheral syllables'; 'Heavy and light syllables in Zaiwa correspond to stressed and unstressed syllables'; '(78) [+stress] = μμ [-stress] = μ'; §6.7 stress and tone = emotional emphasis raising pitch and loudness. Lustig 2010 (excerpt): stressing a syllable = changing its tone to /55/ with weakening of a second syllable to /11/ (calling names, emphasis). 'Every syllable is also specified for tone. There are three tone levels, which combine to form six contour tonemes (listed in Table 2.1).... Tone sandhi is extensive; in this paper, tones are reported in their "surface" or phonetic forms.' Table 2.1: HH 55, MM 33, HM 53, ML 31, MH 35, LM 13. Handel 2003 (review of Sun, Huang & Zhou 2002, author preprint, Chapter 2 summary): 'Rouruo is tonal, so that each syllable is pronounced with a lexically determined distinctive pitch contour.'... 'Both dialects have six tones: two level tones (55 and 33), two falling tones (53 and 31), and two rising tones (35 and 13). There are complex tone sandhi phenomena, which are unfortunately not described.' Miyagishi 2020 p. 21 §2: '声調を持つ点でも，同じく孤立語的である中国語と一致する' [in having tones, too, it agrees with Chinese, likewise an isolating language]; fn. 1 lists the six tone values. Tone does morphological work (noun/verb pairs by tone change, Miyagishi & Li 2018 p. 17). Hull 2023 p. 46 notes that Li 2020 pp. 78-86 discusses 'some aspects of Zauzou intonation' -- the one place a prominence statement might exist; unopened.

5122.dq: Based on my data, there are a total of five tonal melodies at word level. The words that I use to analyze the tonal melodies are only simple words without complex structure, or suffixed words are not used. (p. 58) [Hayward 1990, as reported on p. 52: 'a tonal-accent language in which tone and accent interact at the phrasal level'; Bogale does not analyse that interaction.]

5122.prule: No stress rule. Two-tone (H, L) language, TBU = vowel, tone phonemic with lexical and grammatical functions. Every lexical noun and adjective carries exactly one H, on the ultimate or the penultimate vowel, lexically fixed and 'not predictable'; polysyllabic (3+ syllable) nouns, verbs and adjectives place the H on the penultimate ('bear a high tone on their penultimate syllable', p. 55; 'allow a high tone accent in their second or penultimate syllables', pp. 56-57); disyllabic verbs H on first or last syllable; pronouns carry more than one H. Five word-level melodies on simple unsuffixed words: L, LL, H, HH, LHL. Hayward 1990 (as reported by Bogale p. 52) and Azeb Amha 2014 (first-hand, p. 170) analyse the language as tonal-accent (pitch-accent) 'because of the predictable distribution and restrictions on high tone in multisyllabic words' (Azeb Amha's words); Bogale herself calls it a tonal language and does not adopt the accent analysis.

5122.tone: Bogale 2017 (first-hand): 'Zaysete is a tonal language' with H and L, contour tones on long vowels/diphthongs analysed as HH/HL/LH/LL sequences, tone phonemic (minimal pairs, ex. 152-155) with lexical and grammatical functions. Lexical nouns/adjectives: exactly one H, ultimate or penultimate, unpredictable; 3+-syllable words H on the penultimate; pronouns >1 H. The only stress statement in the dissertation is second-hand: Mulugeta 1988:30 (per Bogale p. 52) says the stress pattern is associated with the pitch pattern (stronger stress = higher pitch), two pitch levels, tone never mentioned; a full-text search of the 368-page dissertation for stress/accent/prominence finds no other stress statement. Hayward 1990 (per Bogale p. 52) calls it a tonal-accent language with isolated-word contours LL, HH, LH, HL, LHL and tone-accent interaction at the phrasal level; Azeb Amha 2014 p. 170: 'Contrast in tone is attested in some words (e.g., Reesé [scan as saved; the intended form is presumably keesé] "a house" vs. kéewe "to bid prices"); however, Zg.-Zs. are analysed as tone-accent languages because of the predictable distribution and restrictions on high tone in multisyllabic words.' Tone vs pitch-accent is the open analytic question between the sources; neither gives a stress rule.

5123.prule: Word-tone language ('African' type) with a culminative accent: each minimal prosodic word has exactly one accented syllable, final or penultimate (right-edge two-syllable window); the position is lexically specified for nouns and lexically/morphologically determined for verbs (static oxytone/perispomenon/paroxytone stems vs kinetic stems alternating final~penult by prefix combination). Final-accented words contrast level tone (oxytone, with glottal constriction) vs falling tone (perispomenon); penult-accented words have no tone contrast. No syllable-count or weight rule for the accent position.
5123.srule: None within the prosodic word: the minimal prosodic word is culminative — 'il n’y a qu’une seule syllabe accentuée avec le ton haut ou haut-tombant. Ainsi, *kə́kəkə́ʔ et *kə́kə̂ sont des formes exclues' (p. 87; cf. §38 p. 75 'Le mot prosodique minimum comporte une seule syllabe accentuée'). Two accented syllables occur only in non-welded compound prosodic words (compound nouns e.g. kəɲɐ̂ʁ-dídi 'pois noir', dvandva, counted nouns with an accented numeral prefix, §41-§43), each member keeping its own lexical accent. No rhythmic/secondary stress described (ch. 3 'Ton et accent', pp. 74-98, read in full).

5123.tone: The author classifies Zbu as a tonal language of the word-tone ('African') type but stresses that it differs from most Sino-Tibetan tone languages 'par l’importance d’une position accentuée avec les corrélats usuels d’un accent dynamique (stress)'; footnote 1 (p. 74) follows Hyman (2009) in refusing the label 'pitch accent'. Acoustic correlates (pp. 76-77): F0 is the most distinct correlate; intensity/duration ('accent dynamique') is asymmetric — barely perceptible for final accent (oxytone/perispomenon), strongly marked for the paroxytone (final unaccented syllable much shorter and weaker, often breathy or devoiced); laryngeal state in pausa (glottal constriction for oxytones, lax/devoiced ending for perispomenon and paroxytone). Pre-accent syllables show a slight rise or stay flat. The two-way tone contrast (level vs falling) exists only on final-accented words.

5125.dq: When a word is unaccented, and contains more than one syllable, greater stress should be put on the first than on any of the others,—thus, “chûnâ,” “now.” [...] In compound words of three or more syllables, the lesser accent rests on the first and the greater on the middle
5125.dloc: Outline Kachcha Naga Grammar, Part I, §3 'Accents', General Rules 1, 2 and 5, printed grammar pp. 3-4 (dli.csl.6760)
5125.prule: Accent placement is set by morphological class and affix identity: an 'unaccented' word of two or more syllables takes the greater stress on the first syllable (General Rule 1), but verbs in conjugation and adjectives with verbal terminations take it on the last (conjugational) syllable; compounds of three or more syllables carry the lesser accent on the first and the greater on the middle syllable (Rule 2); the interrogative particle -mê 'almost invariably' takes the greater accent and the iterative infix -dai- takes the stress; disyllabic nouns move the accent from the first to the second syllable when case-endings are affixed (mi′nâ -> minâ′-kî), trisyllabic nouns do not (hâ′râg″di -> hâ′râg″di-kî) (Rule 5).
5125.srule: Soppitt marks two degrees of accent, the greater (″) and the lesser (′). In compound words of three or more syllables the lesser accent is on the first syllable and the greater on the middle (Hai′gâm″bau; likewise hâ′râg″di 'tiger', tâ′dai″gû 'will go again', tâ′gû mê″ 'will you go?'); with both -dai- and interrogative mê the lesser accent is on dai and the greater on mê (tâ-dai′-gû-mê″). Simple unaccented words carry a single (initial) stress; no rhythmic secondary stress is described.
5125.quote: General Rules. 1. When a word is unaccented, and contains more than one syllable, greater stress should be put on the first than on any of the others,—thus, “chûnâ,” “now.” Exceptions—(a)—Verbs in conjugation have, as a rule, the stress placed on the last syllable, e.g., “tâgû″,” “will go.” (b)—Adjectives when used with verbal terminations follow the above rule, and take the accent on the last syllable, thus “idâ″,” “is good.” 2. 5125.tone: Soppitt 1885 says nothing about tone; his 'greater' and 'lesser' accents are described as stress. Every modern primary description treats Zeme as a lexical tone language and has no stress or accent statement (a full-text search of the saved chapter texts: 'stress'/'accent' absent): Raguibou 2015 ch. 3 'There are three contrastive tones in Zeme. They are high /’/, mid...'; Chanu 2017 ch. 3 line 72 'Zeme has two tones i.e., raising and falling'; Muchahary 2019 ch. 3 'There are three tones in Zeme Naga i.e. rising, level and falling'. Soppitt's accent marks on suffixes and particles (the future suffix -gû, the question particle -mê) may well transcribe tone or intonation rather than stress.

5126.dq: All monosyllables in isolation are uttered in a high (variably level or slightly falling) pitch. With polysyllabic words, a system of stress accent is at work ... Stress commonly falls on the last syllable of the stem
5126.dloc: §2.4 Suprasegmentals, pp. 777–779; examples p. 778; minimal pair and fn. 13 p. 779; corroboration §2.1 p. 771 (elision of ə in unstressed grammatical suffixes) stress marks transcribed from renders of pp. 10–11.
5126.prule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the STEM in polysyllabic words; grammatical suffixes and clitics (-no LOC, -tsə-kə INDEF-INST, -kə MIR, -rə, mə- IMP) are unstressed, so the word-level position is set by the stem/affix boundary (dé-kə initial, l̥ɐsɐ́-no penult, χse-ná final) rather than by word syllable count.
5126.srule: Not mentioned in Sun 2003, §2.4 Suprasegmentals pp. 777-779 (each example word, up to four syllables, carries a single stress mark; nothing is said about secondary or rhythmic stress).
5126.quote: Zhongu makes no phonological use of vocalic length or nasalization, nor is tone lexically significant. All monosyllables in isolation are uttered in a high (variably level or slightly falling) pitch. With polysyllabic words, a system of stress accent is at work, much as we find in such Amdo dialects as Xiámàn 轄曼 (<Byams.me>; J. Sun 1986) and Hóngyuán 紅原 (<dMar.thang>; Huang 1995). As an expected effect of stress accent, the unstressed (and low-toned) vowel ə in Zhongu often weakens and becomes elided in casual speech (see §2.1). Stress commonly falls on the last syllable of the stem, for exam…

5126.exq_: Complex verbs containing nominal roots or complement verbs exhibit trochaic stress instead ... As shown by the minimal pair below, however, stress placement is not always predictable and must sometimes be lexically marked: mé-rə ‘ideophone mimicking moving currents’ / me-rə́ ‘to be red’
5126.tone: 'nor is tone lexically significant'; Zhongu is called 'a cluster and toneless dialect' (§4 p. 796 per the compilers). Monosyllables in isolation are high-pitched; unstressed syllables are low-toned (pitch is a correlate of stress, not lexical). No vowel length or nasalization contrasts.

tn.translation: Stress in Zialo is of the dynamic type, fixed, and falls mostly on the last syllable of the root. Stress is not distorted by tone or by vowel length ... Tone in Zialo is a phonological (meaning-distinguishing) category and plays a most important role in the morphosyntactic system. ... Two level tones are distinguished in Zialo: high and low. The bearer of tone is the vowel. The segmental base of tone is not the syllable but the metrical foot, which in general corresponds to the word. ... A super-high tone has so far been noted only on the conjunction hã̋ 'until'.

tn.note: Two level tones (H, L); a super-high noted on one conjunction only. Tone domain stated as the metrical foot (~word); much grammatical tone; fixed root-final stress said to be independent of tone.

5131.dq: Ivanow 1935 p. 48: 'The accent is fairly mobile, and, as in many dialects, it does not observe the rule of LP of falling on the end of the word.' DLP 2003 Summary p. 28: 'the pronouns form their own stress domains and receive their own word stress.'

Further accent remarks (scan only): p. 54 [24], p. 60 [30], p. 72 [42], p. 79 [49], p. 83 [53], p. 85 [55]. 5131.prule: No positional rule stated by the dedicated description. Ivanow 1935 p. 48: the accent is 'fairly mobile', does not follow the Literary Persian (LP) final-stress rule, and is on the first syllable 'only in some verbal forms'; it is realised by a mix of pitch raising and lengthening 'depending on intonation'. Morphological accent-attractors are named piecemeal: the definite suffix -é 'attracts the accent upon itself' (p. 60), the preverb bar 'is emphatic, attracting the accent' (p. 72), the durative prefix e- 'is stressed, and pronounced as i-' 'sometimes in YG, and almost always in KG' (p. 83) but under emphatic future meaning 'receives some stress... (it does not attract the accent upon itself, however)' (p. 79), LP-style bi- in biure/biwre 'is sharply accented' (p. 83), and the 3sg ending -uné has é 'semi-accented (as the real accent rests on the word itself)' (p. 85). The only fixed-position statements are the Dari Language Project parentheticals: 2003 Preliminary Report '(stress is always on the first syllable of the word)', narrowed by the same authors in the 2003 Summary of Findings to '(stress in Dari is always on the first syllable of a verb)'; both are asides inside a clitichood argument, and the authors' own accented forms m-e-t-ɑ́ 'he gives it to me' and e-vɛ́n-ɑ 'he throws it to us' (verb word beginning with the unstressed continuous prefix e-, which they call a verbal affix) contradict the literal verb-word-initial reading. No catalog rule can be lifted.
5131.srule: Not mentioned in Ivanow 1935 (RSO 16), II.A Phonology p. 48 and the accent remarks on pp. 54-85: no secondary or rhythmic word stress is described. The only graded-accent remarks are morpheme-specific: the emphatic-future prefix e- 'receives some stress... (it does not attract the accent upon itself, however)' (p. 79) and the enclitic 3sg -uné with é 'semi-accented (as the real accent rests on the word itself)' (p. 85). Not mentioned in Toosarvandani & Farudi 2003 either.

5133.idn: The speech of Longzhou city proper (龍州城內的話 / Li's 'Lungchow Dialect... spoken in the city of Lungchow'), Longzhou county, SW Guangxi -- a named variety of Glottolog zuoj1238 Zuojiang Zhuang [zzj] (which also covers Ningming, Chongzuo, Daxin, Tiandeng, Pingxiang); Li 1977 section 1.5 condenses Li 1940.…
5133.tone: Tone language. Li 1977 §1.5.5 'Tones' (Lungchow): 'There are six tones in Lungchow: 1. mid level 33 2. mid falling from mid to low 31 3. high level 55 4. low level 11 5. rising from mid-low to mid-high 24 6. low falling from mid-low to low 21' (two-column list; the Google scan serves item 6's label after item 5's), 'The sixth tone is always accompanied by a glottal stop'; and 'Lungchow divides its syllables into two types: those that end in a vowel or a nasal, and those that end in a stop consonant (except the glottal stop, cf. supra). The first type may have any of the six tones, but the second type only two - tone 3, namely the high level tone 55, or tone 2, namely the mid falling tone 31.' On stress Li says only (§1.5.8) that the dialect 'does not have a strong contrast between different stresses' and that no specific study has been made of its stress patterns or of its intonation; he does not deny stress outright, so the record is tonal rather than no-word-stress. Contrast Li's Po-ai section (§1.6.6, a Northern Tai dialect, not zzj): 'This dialect does not have a prominent stress accent although certain enclitics, such as final particles, are usually less stressed' -- that enclitic remark is NOT made for Lungchow.
